strengths: MaskSub is a simple, technically coherent training modification: a supervised full-input pass supplies detached targets for a masked pass sharing the same parameters. It adds no inference-time parameters. Its practical usefulness and substantial empirical support favor weak acceptance.

The core ImageNet results are convincing across strong recipes and model sizes. Table 1 reports gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points after 400 epochs and 0.3–0.5 after 800 epochs. Repeated runs support the improvement: Table A.13 reports ViT-B accuracy increasing from 83.46 ± 0.04 to 84.08 ± 0.02.

The paper meaningfully addresses additional training cost. Table 8 shows ViT-B reaching 84.1% versus 83.7% using 25 versus 26 GPU days. Table 9 also shows better accuracy than CoSub with lower measured training cost. These comparisons strengthen the contribution beyond gains obtained by spending more compute.

Evaluation is unusually broad, covering supervised training, pretrained-model fine-tuning, hierarchical architectures, transfer classification, segmentation, detection, and robustness. Table A.4 shows consistent improvements across several distribution shifts, including ImageNet-A increasing from 36.8% to 41.9% for ViT-B.

Mask-ratio, loss-weight, and regularization-variant ablations help establish practical behavior. Algorithm 1, detailed training recipes in Tables B.1–B.2, and three-run statistics for several central experiments provide substantial reproducibility support.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is narrower than the framing suggests. With detached teacher predictions, Eq. (3) differs from KL consistency regularization only by a teacher-entropy term that contributes no gradient. Consequently, the stated distinction from UDA based on 'distillation' versus 'consistency' does not establish a different learning objective. The strongest contribution is the effective integration of masking and existing training recipes.

The automatic difficulty-control explanation is not established by the analysis. Aggregate gradient norms in Figure 2 are consistent with the proposed interpretation, but do not demonstrate that masking effectively targets successfully learned examples. Eq. (3) also supervises confidently incorrect predictions. Moreover, zero masking already improves accuracy from 77.4% to 78.4% in Table A.7, indicating a substantial contribution from mechanisms beyond strong masking.

The claims of improvement across all cases overstate applicability. Adding MaskSub during fine-tuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89% to 89.55% in Table A.10. Section 4.2 explicitly states that CLIP's best-checkpoint accuracy is unchanged, despite better final-epoch results. Several GLUE tasks also regress. These results support benefits under particular training schedules, rather than uniformly better attainable performance.

Uncertainty reporting is uneven. Although repeated runs substantiate the main ViT training gains, the 0.1-point BEiTv2 improvements and 0.2/0.3-point COCO improvements lack corresponding variability estimates. These smaller secondary results provide weaker evidence than the central ImageNet experiments.

There are correctable reporting issues: Table A.6 does not clearly specify whether 'without KD loss' replaces distillation with ground-truth supervision or removes the auxiliary objective, which affects interpretation of this ablation. Table 7 also labels both CIFAR columns as CIFAR100. These issues are distinct from the substantive novelty and mechanism concerns.
